# Introduction

#### Research context

-   Handwriting varies across individuals and across writing sessions

-   Despite this variability, individuals may retain distinctive handwriting characteristics

-   The study investigates whether neural networks can identify writers from handwritten digit images

#### Research questions

-   Can a writer be identified by a single handwritten digit?

-   Can a model determine whether two handwritten digits belong to the same writer?

#### Approach

-   Convolutional Neural Network

-   Siamese Neural Network

# Exploratory Data Analysis

### Visual findings

```{r}
#| echo: false
library(dplyr)
library(knitr)

data <- readRDS("handwriting.rds")
meta <- data$metadata
X <- matrix(data$images, nrow = 25000) / 255
images <- data$images

s <- 1
selected_persons <- c(1, 9, 18)

# Set up a plotting grid: 3 rows (one for each person) and 5 columns (for the 5 sessions)
par(mfrow = c(length(selected_persons), 5), mar = c(0.5, 0.5, 1, 0.5))

for (p in selected_persons) {
  for (d in 0:4) {
    # Find the index matching the person, digit, and session
    matching_indices <- which(meta$person_id == p & meta$digit == d & meta$session == s)
    
    if (length(matching_indices) > 0) {
      i <- matching_indices[1]
      image(t(data$images[i,,,1])[, 28:1], axes = FALSE, col = gray.colors(256),
            main = paste("Person", p, "| S", s))
    } else {
      # Plot an empty blank space if a specific combination is missing
      plot.new()
      title(main = paste("Person", p, "| S", s))
    }
  }
}

# Reset plotting parameters back to default
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

### Visual findings

-   Different writers display visible handwriting characteristics that could help a model identify them

-   Handwriting varies within the same person, but certain individual characteristics persist across sessions

-   A writer's style can be expressed across different digits, potentially helping a model recognise a person even when the digit changes

|diff_writer_diff_session |    8.79 |    7.85 |    8.10 |    8.18 |    7.98 |

Table. Euclidean Distances and Ratios Across Digits (0 to 4)

-   There is a measurable signal for distinguishing writers, but handwriting changes between sessions enough to make identification challenging

-   The similarity of distances for different writers within and across sessions also supports the finding that there is little overall session effect

# Siamese Neural Network

## Methods

### General Siamese structure

-   Input: 2 images

-   Uses a CNN

-   Output: distance between embeddings of images

-   Distance infers dissimilarity

-   Contrastive loss:

$$L = yD^2 + (1-y)max(0, m-D)^2$$

### Metrics

#### Sensitivity

-   Proportion of actual positive cases correctly identified $$\text{Sensitivity} = \frac{\text{True Positives}}{\text{True Positives + False Negatives}}$$

#### Specificity

-   Proportion of actual negative cases correctly identified $$\text{Specificity} = \frac{\text{True Negatives}}{\text{True Negatives + False Positives}} $$

#### Balanced accuracy

-   Accounts for imbalanced classes $$\text{Balanced Accuracy} = \frac{\text{Sensitivity + Specificity}}{2}$$

### Default calibration

| Hyperparameter         | Value                |
|:-----------------------|:---------------------|
| Hidden layers          | 2                    |
| Activation functions   | ReLU                 |
| Number of filters      | 16 and $2 \times 16$ |
| Filter size            | $3 \times 3$         |
| Learning rate          | $1 \times 10^{-3}$   |
| Dropout rate           | 0.2                  |
| L2 regularisation      | $1 \times 10^{-3}$   |
| Layer 1 pooling window | $2 \times 2$         |
| Embedding length       | 16                   |
| Epochs                 | 15                   |

### Tuning

-   Hidden layers
-   Activation functions
-   Filter (square) size
-   Number of filters
-   Average validation performance metrics reported

## Results

### Tuning hidden layers

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
hidden_layer_tune <- data.frame(
  `Number of Hidden Layers` = c(1, 2),
  `Validation Loss` = c(0.214, 0.105),
  `Balanced Accuracy` = c(0.773, 0.966),
  check.names = FALSE
)

hidden_layer_tune |>
  kable(
    format = "latex",
    booktabs = TRUE,
    align = c("r", "r", "r")
  )
```

### Tuning activation functions

```{r}

#| message: false
#| warning: false

act_fn_tune <- data.frame(
  `Activation Functions` = c(

# Display the table and highlight relu_tanh
act_fn_tune |>
  kable(
    format = "latex",
    booktabs = TRUE,
    align = c("l", "r", "r")

  row_spec(
    which(act_fn_tune$`Activation Functions` == "relu_tanh"),
    background = "yellow!45"
  )
```

### Final model

#### Tuned inputs

-   Hidden layers: 2
-   Activation functions: reLU and tanh
-   Filter (square) size: $5 \times 5$
-   Number of filters: 16 and 32
-   Epochs: 6

#### Outputs

-   Test Balanced accuracy: 0.820
-   Test Loss: 0.104
-   Distance threshold: 0.247

# Discussion


### CNN accuracy

-   Achieved 55.0% writer identification accuracy, well above the 5% random-guessing baseline

-   Outperformed the linear baseline by 11.4 percentage points

-   Similar accuracy to the default CNN, but substantially better probability calibration (cross-entropy: 1.39 vs. 5.87)

-   Test accuracy had a wide confidence interval of 42.7%–67.1%, indicating uncertainty

### CNN model limitations

-   Accuracy varied significantly between writers, ranging from 0% to 100%

-   Misclassifications were systematic, with similar-looking digits often assigned to the same incorrect writer

-   Cross-session handwriting variation made a writer's new samples resemble another writer's training samples

-   Tuning reduced the training–validation accuracy gap from 55 to 26 percentage points, but overfitting remained

-   The test accuracy of 55.0% is more reliable than the 60.4% validation accuracy


### Siamese accuracy

-   Performed well when identifying pairs of handwriting samples from the same session

-   Performance declined substantially when comparing handwriting across different sessions

-   Cross-session balanced accuracy fell to 55.4%, only slightly above the 50% random-guessing baseline

-   Sensitivity dropped to 11.2%, indicating difficulty identifying samples written by the same person across sessions

-   Validation performance may overestimate real-world reliability because validation data did not fully represent session variability

### Siamese model limitations

-   Sequential hyperparameter tuning may have overlooked interactions between parameters

-   The final model performed worse than the tuning models, suggesting the selected combination may not have been optimal

-   Repeated tuning on the same validation set may have produced overly optimistic performance estimates

-   Differences in session representation across training, validation and test datasets complicated generalisation

# Conclusion


### Conclusion

-   Both models struggled with cross-session handwriting variation

-   The CNN could identify writers above chance, but its accuracy was not sufficiently reliable

-   The Siamese network distinguished same-session pairs more effectively than cross-session pairs

-   Variation in an individual's handwriting across sessions appears to be the main obstacle to reliable writer recognition
